title: You Always Do This
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership piece addresses what happens when a leader spots a recurring negative behavior in someone else and decides to raise it. The author argues that noticing the pattern is fine; the damage comes from phrasing it in absolutes such as always and never. Absolutes leave the other person no room to explain, and stacking up examples only deepens the defensiveness, so the person either counterattacks or withdraws. The proposed alternative is to name the cause-and-effect link in plain terms, along the lines of when this happens you often do that, without implying the flaw is permanent. The move is a small wording discipline for feedback conversations about repeated behavior.
points: Calling out a pattern is legitimate; the failure is in turning the observation into a sweeping verdict about the person.
Absolute words remove the listener's chance to explain, which pushes them toward attack or withdrawal.
Piling on additional examples intensifies defensiveness rather than proving the point.
A workable script is to connect the dots between a trigger and the typical response without labeling the behavior as irreversible.
quotes: Statements like, “You always…” or “You never…” are highly tempting to those who recognize a pattern. But those statements box people in, with little hope for a rational response. When leaders pile on by offering a litany of examples, instances, and illustrations, they make the situation even more tense.

When confronted with a pattern via statements of “Always” and “Never,” people become wildly defensive. The more the leader elaborates, offering even more examples to prove their point, the more defensive the other party will typically become.

In the absence of any rational rebuttal to such a strong statement, the other party resorts to what they perceive as their only option. They attack the accuser or withdraw from the conversation altogether. The end result is usually a nasty conflict.
Recognizing and calling out a pattern is not the problem. Rather, the issue stems from denying others the possibility of explaining themselves. “Always” and “Never” rob them of this option.
Good leaders refrain from casting patterns as absolute. They flag the cause-and-effect patterns they see without painting them as permanent or historically inescapable.
